consensus_summary: The helmet of salvation is the believer’s assurance or hope of salvation that protects the mind against doubt, despair, and spiritual attack, as part of God’s armor; primary texts are Eph 6:17, 1 Thess 5:8 and Isa 59:17.
book_summary: The head covered with yeshuah—Yeshua: God’s own war-dress put on when there was no man and lent to the soldier; David’s form (“thou hast covered my head in the day of battle”); the head of every man is Christ, and the counterfeit is issued for the same forehead.
consensus_core_identification: assurance/hope of salvation as protective covering for the believer’s mind in spiritual warfare
book_core_identification: covering of the head with yeshuah/Yeshua as God’s own war-dress lent to the soldier, the head being Christ (with forehead counterfeit)
boundary_disagreement: Book equates yeshuah with the person Yeshua, applies 1 Cor 11:3 (head of every man is Christ) and Rev 22:4 forehead imagery (plus counterfeit), reclassifying the symbol christologically and as a seal; consensus primary centers psychological assurance/hope and treats divine-warrior or Christ-as-armor readings as secondary alternatives.
rationale: Both cores identify the helmet with salvation drawn from God’s own armor (Isa 59) and given for the believer’s protection (Eph 6); the divine-warrior motif and “salvation as Christ” are already listed consensus alternatives. The book therefore preserves the central referent while refining its precision and extension through the yeshuah=Yeshua identification, the headship of Christ, and the forehead-counterfeit contrast—producing real boundary disagreement without replacing the referent.
strongest_objection: Consensus primary meaning stresses present assurance or future hope as mental protection; the book’s christological equation and counterfeit-forehead extension, while drawing on printed texts, shift emphasis beyond the armor passages themselves.
